Quantisation. The fundamental principle that certain physical quantities—particularly energy, angular momentum, and electric charge—can only take discrete values rather than continuous ranges. Discovered through quantum mechanics, quantisation reveals that at atomic scales, nature operates in fundamental chunks or quanta, profoundly violating classical intuition and underlying nearly all of modern physics.

Energy is quantised. Atoms can only occupy specific energy levels, not arbitrary energies. Transitions between levels involve absorption or emission of photons with precise frequencies. Angular momentum is quantised. Electrons in atoms have orbital angular momenta that are integer multiples of h-bar, explaining why atoms remain stable and don't collapse into the nucleus. Electric charge is quantised. All charge in the universe is an integer multiple of the elementary charge, approximately 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth coulombs. This fact was demonstrated by Millikan's oil-drop experiment. Planck's constant, equal to 6.63 times ten to the negative thirty-fourth joule-seconds, sets the scale of quantisation. The quantum of energy is energy equals Planck's constant times frequency. Quantisation explains atomic spectra. Atoms absorb and emit photons of only specific wavelengths because transitions occur only between discrete energy levels. The Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrates quantisation of spin angular momentum. A beam of atoms splits into discrete spots, not a continuous spread, revealing quantised spin states. Quantisation is not merely an approximation at small scales. It is a fundamental feature of nature, giving rise to chemistry, solid-state physics, and most of modern technology. Quantisation is explained by quantum mechanics, the theoretical framework predicting and explaining these discrete effects.
